claims.claim: Elliott describes the betrothal chapter as an assassin's survey of an institutional occasion, with the narrator marking entrances and behaviours as nobles gather and assessing each party as it arrives.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 1 December 2021
claims.quote: marking entrances and behaviors as minor nobles flock to Lord Golden

claims.claim: Elliott records that the chapter opens with an in-milieu reflection on the office of King- or Queen-in-Waiting, which he glosses against the Prince of Wales and the Dauphin.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 30 August 2019
claims.quote: an in-milieu reflection on the position of King/Queen-in-Waiting

claims.claim: Elliott says a sense of being rushed is something he has noted in several of Hobb's works, and calls this chapter's reversal of the narrator's intent hurried.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, Elliott RWI, 30 August 2019
claims.quote: A sense of being rushed is something I have noted

claims.claim: Oliver characterises the register of the chapter epigraphs in Assassin's Apprentice as a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice, set against an undefined, reminiscent main narrative.
Oliver quotes the novel's first epigraph as opening with the authoritative voice of History declaring that a history of the Six Duchies is necessarily a history of its ruling family.
claims.quote: A history of the Six Duchies is of necessity a history
claims.page: p. 53, section 'Historical Authority in Assassin's Apprentice'

claims.claim: Oliver names the book's most striking stylistic element a style of negative narration, in which the prose says what is not happening instead of, or before, what is.
claims.quote: a style we might think of as “negative narration.”

claims.claim: Oliver says the negative construction appears in Assassin's Apprentice not only as double negatives, of which he says there are many, but in sentences that open by saying what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.quote: just in double negatives (of which there are many)

claims.claim: Oliver reports the density of the device in the early chapters of Assassin's Apprentice, saying scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples, and that its frequency lessens as the novel continues.
claims.quote: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples

claims.claim: Oliver identifies the elevated style associated with fantasy novels as extensive parataxis together with elevated figurative language and parallelism, and shows the narrator switching into it when he invents a vision.
claims.quote: elevated style associated with fantasy novels, particularly extensive parataxis

claims.claim: Oliver argues the narrator keeps the style of the epigraphs and the style of the main text separate for most of the novel, and that a poetic lyricism later creeps into the epigraph as a signal of contamination.
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver argues the novel inverts the usual priority of document and testimony: the authoritative scholarly history sits in the margins while the personal narrative is the main text, which he calls the marginalia.
claims.quote: The main text is the marginalia

claims.claim: Oliver reports that the objective history opening each chapter reads as dry and impersonal, and feels less authoritative and satisfying to the reader than the personal narrative that follows it.
Oliver reports that other critics treat the fictional epigraph as a genre tic rather than a virtue, citing Diana Wynne Jones's satire of Gnomic Utterances in The Tough Guide to Fantasyland.
claims.quote: Wynne Jones satirizes the use of “Gnomic Utterances”

claims.claim: Oliver notes that the main text of Assassin's Apprentice reveals the epigraph's author and the first-person narrator to be one person, which bears on how reliable that history can be.
claims.quote: the  epigraph  author  and  first-person  narrator  are  the  same
claims.page: p. 53, section 'Historical Authority in Assassin's Apprentice'

claims.claim: Oliver's abstract states the structural effect of the device: prefacing each chapter with an epigraph from an official in-world historical text before a first-person personal narrative blurs the boundary between official history and personal myth-making.
